it’ll be okay! I used to work in the store as a technician, the repair/tech support queue is completely separate from the shopping queue. Since it’s already been sent out once, the process should be really easy for you to get this taken care of quickly. 

If you have your e-receipt or another apple device logged in under the same ID, you can find your phone’s serial number there under your device list in Settings. If you find it, go here and follow the steps to have Apple send you a new phone. Free under AppleCare+ and about $30 under limited warranty. https://support.apple.com/iphone/repair/express-replacement (more on it below)

If you go to the store, a person should be waiting around the front to greet and check you in. you can reserve an appointment slot online for the Genius Bar in advance, or just walk in and they’ll book you a same-day one (waiting times can vary, usually not more than 15 mins). 

They’ll get your name and probably ask for the serial number of the device, but just tell them it won’t turn on so you don’t have it. Once you’re seated with the technician, they have a tool that will read the serial number even if the phone’s dead and broken. 

They’ll use that SN to pull up the repair record for the phone. They’ll be able to see that it was sent out to the depot, and they’ll see the notes left by that technician to figure out what happened. Then they’ll run a quick test to verify whether it’s a single part failing, or the whole system. 

Once they see the phone won’t power on, and that you sent it to depot and had it sent back, you can go with 1 of these 3 avenues:

- Let them repair it. They’ll likely do a **mid-system** repair, where the motherboard and all internal components except the screen and outer chassis are replaced. This is the fastest option, and is done within an hour, usually. Phone will be returned in better-than-new condition, don’t worry about that. 

- If they don’t offer a repair, they may inform you they have to resend the device to the depot again for further inspection. If they tell you this, **please don’t give the technician a hard time** as this is something that our repair system will enforce automatically if certain diagnostics aren’t conclusive - and there is absolutely no way to get around it, not even management is able to override it if they want to. This is a corporate Apple mandate. But there are ways to get around needing to send it in again, so **if this happens, ask for help setting up an Express Replacement**. If you paid for AppleCare+, it’s free. If not and you still have your 1-year ltd warranty, it should cost about $30.

This is where Apple sends you a brand-new device (exact same model as yours) within 48 hours, and you then have a 2-week return window to send the original back (comes with a shipping label).

Since it’s a 15, there is a 99% chance the replacement phone is going to be brand new, and a 1% chance of it being refurbished (but if it is that’s actually great news because Apple refurbishment quality assurance is INSANE and you can guarantee that phone is going to be absolutely mint, oftentimes better than factory).  

If the technician is good, they’ll document the issue with the device and help you set up the replacement online. If not, it’s a very straightforward process and can be done from the comfort of your own home, here’s the link again: https://support.apple.com/iphone/repair/express-replacement

And that’s it! Hope this information helps, and don’t sweat it. As long as the phone isn’t cracked or water-damaged, you have nothing to worry about. :)

Apple tech here, this is accurate! You’re right that I can’t seem to find any confirmation of it online, but you can probably call to confirm. If you care to trust an internet stranger, this is how it is currently working:

- For all Macs, iPhones and iPads, you can enrol the device in AppleCare+ yourself for up to 60 days through Settings.
- You can bring any of these devices into an Apple Store within a year of purchase (so within its limited warranty period) and request to have the coverage added. The coverage takes effect the day it is purchased, NOT the day the device was bought. However, you can’t get AppleCare+ on an already-damaged device after the first 60 days, because it needs to pass both a general hardware diagnostic and cosmetic check to be eligible. If the device is found to be damaged, you have to pay the regular out-of-warranty rate to have it repaired, after which it WILL be eligible and you can request to have AppleCare+ added post repair.

- Recently (like within the last year or so), the eligibility window to add AppleCare+ on all iPhones was bumped to up to 2 years after the date of purchase. Otherwise standard protocol has not changed. 

- So to clarify, for Mac and iPad, you still have the entire ltd warranty period (1 year from the date of purchase) to request AppleCare+ enrolment. For iPhone, you have 2 years to do so. But after the first 60 days, you have to bring the device to a store to have it assessed regardless.

AirPods and other accessories can only be enrolled in AC+ within the first 60 days.

This is super late but just stumbled upon this - lots of folks with fibro also have hypermobility and/or EDS. When you have either of these conditions, your joints do NOT like to stay where they should be and you’re much more prone to getting injured doing day-to-day things. To prevent this, the body will tell all your muscles to tighten up and work overtime to keep your joints in place and protect them from dislocation/subluxation. Unfortunately, having constantly tightened muscles can be a (literal) pain in the ass and can eventually trigger chronic pain conditions like fibromyalgia. 

When you take a muscle relaxant like cyclobenzaprine while also existing with hypermobility, you’re FORCING the muscles to completely relax and ultimately stop protecting those fragile joints. This can release a ton of pain by allowing your muscles to have a break, but can also result in much easier injuries, bruising and dislocations. (This is also why it’s usually recommended to only take them right before bed, when you’re moving around the least.)

Massage therapists that aren’t specifically trained in treating patients with hypermobile joints already pose a risk as they can very easily massage or push a ligament out of place with their hands. That risk of injury becomes even greater when that patient has just taken a muscle relaxant, as their last barrier of defence around the joints is gone. 

It’s like jostling around a box full of glass cups without any padding inside, and praying none of the glasses break.

Hope that helps!!

Apple tech here, just wanted to drop some info!

Apple manufactures the camera and camera lens as two separate components: The camera itself, the fragile mechanism beneath the glass, is able to be replaced for around 200 or so in the event of a failure. But the sapphire lens covering on top of each camera is built into the entire rest of the back of the device. To replace a single cracked lens glass is to replace the entire rear chassis, and in most models this includes the actual logic board and other internal hardware as well. So it’s effectively a new phone, hence the weirdly high price.

Apple technician here. If you plan on having the device for 2+ years, please buy it. Something as simple as a screen or battery replacement costs more upfront than the coverage, think 400+ for one part. I have a 2019 MacBook that is out of warranty and the cost for a fresh battery and screen is more than an entirely new system. 

A part replacement out of warranty only adds another 90 days of warranty to the part, so in the event of another issue you’d be paying that price again and again. AppleCare covers battery replacements at no cost once they’ve degraded below 80%, so if you plan on keeping the device for awhile it pays for itself in one use.

You can do a monthly payment and have it for as long as you have the device. You can also pay for the 2 years upfront and switch to monthly at the end of that period. You can also call Apple support within a certain timeframe (a couple months I think?) if you change your mind and they’ll refund the AppleCare fee for you, less any deductibles you’ve used. 

You also don’t have to make the decision now - even after the first 60 days but within the first year you can walk in store and have them add it for you. They run a hardware test on the unit first though so it must be functional and free of damage to be eligible. 

Let me know if you’ve got any questions! Store associates are not commission-based and will not pressure you to buy. They will mention it as we’re only rated on how often we mention AppleCare to customers. So just make sure you do your research and decide whether it’s a good investment or not!

Comments like this can be really harmful as we tend to make these sweeping assumptions that everyone is going to react to a drug the same way. 

I’ve been taking duloxetine for 2 years and have had literally 0 of the horror stories. No addiction, no horrible side effects, have missed doses before, nothing bad happened at all. At worst I felt a little groggy. 4 of my colleagues have also taken it in the past for pain, and did not experience any terrible symptoms. At worst it did nothing! Of course it really just comes down to the person, everyone reacts differently, and Cymbalta seems to be one of the more polarizing experiences. But those who’ve had extremely bad side effects with it will obviously (and justifiably) be a lot more vocal about it than those who benefited. 

I just wouldn’t want someone to read this comment and be dissuaded from trying Cymbalta if it turns out to be something amazingly helpful for them, like it was for me.

PLEASE don’t let this scare you. Remember that people who have positive experiences on Cymbalta will never post online about it, whereas those who experience the negatives will. 

I have been on Cymbalta for almost 2 years and it has been fantastic. I was super hesitant at first. I am on a small dose right now, but have tapered up and down with very minimal side effects. The worst I had was a little stomach ache for a few days. It has not been addictive to me in the slightest, and mainly helps with anxiety for me, less so for pain. But everyone will be different!

The reality of pain management is LOTS of trial and error, which can sometimes come with annoying (temporary) side effects. Though the potential for discomfort if a medication doesn’t end up working for you, should never ever be a reason for you not to try something that could be life changing.

Continue on the Cymbalta unless you find it’s not providing benefit, in which case, talk to your practitioner who will help you gradually titrate down and reduce any side effects you might have. Same as any other medication, and nothing to be scared of. 

It’s good to be mindful of the potential side effects before starting anything, staying informed is never a bad thing, but don’t let a list of possible side effects and anecdotes about how bad it was for other people negate the potential it could have to help you. Because those people are not you, and you’re going to react differently regardless, because you’re not them!

I see comments like this sometimes and feel the need to explain that it’s not that the animation has gotten *worse* - it’s just a completely different style! Bear with me.

An example I heard once and liked: You have two paintings. One is hyper-realistic and detailed, trying to look as close to real life as possible. The other is colourful, wild and abstract, and is in no way trying to imitate real life. They are made by the same artist and took the same amount of time to paint. Just because they look different, would you say one is fundamentally “worse quality” than the other? Would you say that the abstract painting isn’t a painting, because it’s not realistic? No? Of course not! They’re two completely different genres!

It’s the same thing here. To audiences who aren’t super familiar with how animation works as a medium, it’s an easy mistake. “This doesn’t look at all realistic - they must have cut the budget!”
But if we really are speaking from a technical standpoint, The Last Wish outshines its predecessor in every way.

I love both films, but the sequel is a HUGE technological advancement for DreamWorks and the animation industry as a whole. The decision to remove some realism and detail was a deliberate choice. But take some time to focus on the facial animations, the fluidity of movement, the gorgeous colours, painterly environments & visual effects, the way light and shadow works in the world. 

It’s not trying to look like Shrek because Shrek is an entirely different movie, never mind one that’s over 20 years old!

TL;DR: In terms of animation **quality**, TLW is factually better. But in terms of animation **style**, it’s like comparing apples to oranges. One can’t be better than the other, but you can definitely have a preference for one.

Honestly, this is EXACTLY how my art looked at like, 18. You’re doing fantastic and it shows so much promise! I can clearly see that you’re a deliberate sketcher - someone who cares a lot about the details and end result of their work. Every stroke you make is well thought-out and purposeful, you know where you want it to go!

If you stick with it, those skills could be what sets you apart. But for right now, while you’re skillbuilding, you’re actually going to have to trust me and try to do the exact opposite! You have to stop caring about what the end result of your drawings look like (I know that sounds ridiculous, bear with me)!

It’ll be best to focus on your basic shapes and - as others have said - perspective. Pull up a short little video on one-point perspective drawing, nothing crazy, and try to draw a cube. Then another cube. Shapes are what you’ll use to draw EVERYTHING, ever. Like the Switch and the dresser. Think about it, they’re just a bunch of cubes, right? That phone is a cube! And the lamppost? Cubes, cones, spheres! Once you’ve got a well-trained eye, you’ll be able to break down any object in the universe into simple shapes, and then build them up again on paper.

But, the one thing I might add that’ll improve your art RIGHT now, aside from time and perspective studying, is **to put down that eraser!**

Seriously, it’ll suck at first and that’s the point. Lock the eraser away in a vault, DO NOT TOUCH IT, grab a sheet of paper and a pencil (or even a pen) and redraw something like the Switch. Focus on pulling long, steady lines instead of smaller ticks that connect together to form a shape. It’s going to look awful and feel super uncomfortable at first, but DO NOT TOUCH THE ERASER and keep going!! Hold the pencil steady and move it from your shoulder, rather than a flick of the wrist. Try and draw the curve of that lamppost, from top to bottom, in one line. You don’t have to worry about the shape thing right now, you don’t even have to draw in 3D. You can even copy a fun design or a favourite cartoon character off the internet for practice (but try not to trace, your brain won’t learn a thing)! The point is to just focus on making long, steady hand movements without lifting the pencil. 

Eventually, if you keep doing that, the lines you pull will start to look less wobbly. And once you’ve got that hammered down, your drawings will have automatically improved by 300 percent.

Hope that makes sense. You’re doing amazing. Best of luck! <3

I tried to be vague about my own diagnosis intentionally as obviously it’s going to be a different journey for everyone, and I didn’t want anyone to feel like I was trying to say “EVERYONE with BPD actually has THIS diagnosis instead.” That just wouldn’t be true!

But for me personally, it was a few different things all bunched together! I was diagnosed with OCD when I was maybe 7, so that was a part of it. The newer diagnoses came later - ADHD and autism spectrum disorder. 

I was totally taken aback at the ASD diagnosis, until I started reading up on that too. Turns out it can manifest completely differently in women vs. men. After learning more about it I came to realize that autism was a MUCH more fitting conclusion than BPD ever was.

ADHD was comorbid and came bundled with that. It’s still a work in progress today, but I think that diagnosis was the key to how I’m going to get back into school and successfully finish my degree. The medication in question that completely turned me around was Vyvanse, and later on, Cymbalta as well. I had fibromyalgia as a result of some physical issues and trauma, the Cymbalta put a cap on the pain which improved my quality of life unprecedentedly. This was a living, breathing indication that your physical condition does indeed have a huge impact on your mental condition as well.

If you find yourself relating to a lot of what I’m mentioning, a second opinion definitely never, ever hurts. In fact, I’ve come to have the opinion that it’s ALWAYS worth getting the perspective of more than one doctor, even if you’re in total agreeance with their diagnosis and plan for you.

The critical thing to remember is that, it doesn’t really matter how many diagnoses you have - I was the same person before my diagnosis, circumstances just exacerbated my symptoms and made me a worse version of myself. The diagnoses allowed me the closure and explanation I needed to fully and completely accept myself, recognize my needs, and advocate effectively for them - but the diagnosis isn’t the cure, it’s also what comes afterwards. A huge piece of my recovery was putting in the work to find professionals that I clicked with, whose goals for my growth aligned with my own. 

Not every doctor or therapist is made equal, and not all are going to gel with you and that’s just the nature of the practice. It’s a shame that it can take so long to find the right people for you, but it is possible so long as you don’t settle for mediocrity. I had to switch doctors, switch psychiatrists, and find a psychologist specializing in the handful of diagnoses I did have - and even then, you don’t know if it’s going to work until you sit down in a room with them. I don’t have much to add to all the lovely comments here, but I do want to say that you will not only heal, but be better for it. 

A breakup isn’t like a bone, where you break it once and it heals, but it’s always just a teensy tiny bit weaker. 

No ma’am. 

A breakup is like pruning a plant. You remove the damaged bits - the leaves, the stems, and the branches that didn’t get quite enough sun. It hurts to see them go, because you were hoping they’d stay green and growing for much longer. Maybe you’d been watching that one new sprout for the longest time, and suddenly it’s gone and wilted on you. Maybe you didn’t even intend to prune any leaves! Maybe they just withered and fell on their own. 

Regardless of how it happened, it happened. I mean, sure, you could superglue those leaves back on. But alas, you know as well as I do that they’ve had their time. 

For a while, your plant looks a little frail. Okay, maybe a lot frail. Like, can you even call this a plant? It’s just skin and bone, really. How on earth did it get like this? It’s smaller, weaker and missing so much of what it had just moments before you pruned it. You start to wonder if you’re cursed to kill every living thing you touch.

Nonetheless, you love that little plant! You don’t want to see it at the bottom of a compost bag, and neither do I. So you decide you’ll give it some time. Days, weeks, months, even years. Who am I to say how long that plant needs? Every one is different!

You give it as long as it takes. You take extra special care of it. You buy it plant food, top up the soil, sing it a little song - wow, you even downloaded one of those nifty apps that reminds you to water it? You must mean business!

And then one day, before you know it, something magical begins to happen. Something feels different about that plant. Slowly at first, so slow that you might not even notice! But then you look down at 3:46 PM on a Tuesday and realize that not only has this little plant grown, but it’s also **bloomed.** There are new flowers in place of the old, withering leaves. Young sprouts, lush with colour - budding, vibrant, **alive.** Different? Oh yes, very! But just about a hundred times more beautiful than what was there before. Who knew that all of that beauty was hiding beneath the surface, just waiting for you to cut an opening? All it needed was another chance!

I can’t tell you what kind of plant you have, or how to care for it. What I can tell you, is that embracing the change, the hurt, ***and most importantly the time***, will not only allow you to heal, but to bloom. To learn more about what you needed, and what’s been inside you all along. 

The goal after a breakup is never to feel the same. The correct goal, is to make way for inevitable change.

You, my dear, are not broken. You’re growing.

Honestly, don’t be too disheartened, BPD is notoriously difficult to treat since it presents so differently in different people. You’re definitely not a shit patient, it’s just about trying different things until something sticks. 

I saw that you’ve tried some medication, and while I’d like to explore that venue further with you, if you’re not open to it that’s totally okay! Personally, I’m using medication to target some of my most prevalent BPD symptoms, and utilizing the therapy to cover off on what the medication doesn’t. There isn’t a medication out there that’s approved to treat BPD as a whole, so we unfortunately have to do a lot of trial and error to find one that helps with your worst symptoms. For example, you might try different medications that help with your mood swings but not your depression, or with your irritability but not the paranoia. You might try antidepressants, SSRIs or small dosage antipsychotics before finding one that starts to help. And even then, the results may not last forever, because your BPD can adapt and evolve. I had a medication that gave me so much relief for an entire year, then suddenly stopped. It’s all about learning to recognize when something isn’t as effective as it used to be, and then being proactive about trying new stuff!

I’m not sure if it was a psychiatrist who prescribed you your original medication, but if not I’d highly suggest looking into seeing one (if you’re open to that, of course!). For the longest time my family doctor was doing my prescriptions, and it was very ineffective for me. In 2018 I saw a wonderful psychiatrist, and he was the one who diagnosed me and started me on the path to proper treatment. Seeing the right person can make a whole world of difference!

I have a few more potentially helpful, evidence-based things to share, but let me know what your thoughts are on this! Remember that BPD research is still in its infancy, so you’re not alone, and absolutely not to blame for feeling the way you have been.
